newsitem.title: USA: Brazil could handle rise in U.S. int rates - Malan.
newsitem.headline: Brazil could handle rise in U.S. int rates - Malan.

text.p: Brazil could easily manage a modest increase in U.S. interest rates as its own credit risk has been declining steadily, Brazilian Finance Minister Pedro Malan said on Tuesday.

Malan told a news conference on the fringes of the IMF/World Bank spring meeting that nobody expects the U.S. Federal Reserve to tighten as much as it did in the 1970s or even in 1994, when a slighter rise in U.S. rates roiled emerging markets.
"So we could afford an increase of 25 or 50 basis points in U.S. rates without major problems," he said.
Malan noted that the interest rate spread of Brazilian bonds over equivalent U.S. treasuries had dropped from about 480 basis points in 1995 to below 240 basis points at present.
Another Brazilian bond launched on Monday in Austrian schillings, French francs and guilders averaged a weighted spread below 200 basis points, he added.
Brazil has also stretched out maturities, from just two years in 1995 to a 20-year issue it is currently mulling.
Malan further argued that investor confidence in Brazil's prospects was best shown by the $11 billion it attracted in foreign direct investment in the 12 months to end-March.
He said that 40 percent of Brazil's current account deficit represented foreign direct investment, and that the rest was largely being financed through long-term loans and bonds.
Furthermore, he stressed that Brazil was not as dependent on short-term capital inflows as some other countries were in the recent past.
Mexico and Argentina suffered severe financial shocks in late 1994 and early 1995 due to a reversal of capital flows.
Malan also said that Brazil would be a "capital importing country for many years to come".
Regarding the public sector deficit, Malan said Brazil's gradual declining trend over the past two years was not very different from Canada's, Britain's, France's or Italy's.

Brazil's fiscal deficit -- which consolidates not only the central government's but the deficits of 27 states, 5,560 municipalities, the social security system and all public sector enterprises -- dipped from 7.05 percent of GDP in 1995 to 6.05 percent in 1996 and stood at 5.75 percent for the year to end-February, he said.
"In other words, the fiscal situation in Brazil is improving. Some people say it is far too gradual, it should be much faster, but it is improving, not deteriorating," he said.
However, he acknowledged that Brazil had to narrow its public sector deficit more quickly than industrialized nations.
"Our sense of urgency is much higher. That is why we have for 1997 a government target of having a primary surplus of 1.5 percent of GDP for the consolidated public sector," Malan said.
IMF and World Bank officials noted during the spring meeting, which wrapped up on Tuesday, that the Brazilian government would have to work harder to close that gap.
